cards.front: What are the five effects on the body of not getting enough protein, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Poor growth / Slow healing / Muscle wasting / Weak immune system / Kwashiorkor

cards.front: Which four groups of people need more protein than the standard adult amount, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Growing children and teenagers / Pregnant and breastfeeding women / People recovering from illness or surgery / Athletes building muscle
items: People recovering from illness or surgery

cards.front: Why do vegetarians and vegans often need to combine different plant protein foods in a meal?
cards.answer: Because most plant proteins are missing one or more essential amino acids, so combining sources supplies all eight together.

cards.front: Why is soya especially important for people on a vegetarian or vegan diet?
cards.answer: It is the only common plant food that is high biological value, supplying all eight essential amino acids by itself.

cards.front: What are the three monosaccharides (simple sugars) named in this lesson?
cards.answer: Glucose / Fructose / Galactose

cards.front: What four functions of fat does this lesson describe?
cards.answer: Provides concentrated energy / Insulates the body / Protects organs from damage / Helps absorb vitamins A, D, E, K
items: Helps absorb vitamins A, D, E, K

cards.front: Why do polysaccharides release energy more slowly than simple sugars?
cards.answer: They are long chains of many sugar units, so the body takes longer to digest them.

cards.front: Why does eating dietary fibre help prevent constipation?
cards.answer: It absorbs water and helps move food through the digestive system, keeping things moving.

cards.front: Which four vitamins are fat-soluble, remembered by the mnemonic ADEK?
cards.answer: Vitamin A / Vitamin D / Vitamin E / Vitamin K

cards.front: What are the three functions of vitamin A described in this lesson?
cards.answer: Vision, especially in dim light / Supports the immune system / Keeps skin and mucous membranes healthy
items: Keeps skin and mucous membranes healthy

cards.front: Why is vitamin C important for wound healing?
cards.answer: It is needed to form collagen, the protein that builds connective tissue in skin and blood vessels.

cards.front: Why does eating vitamin C-rich food alongside iron-rich plant food help the body?
cards.answer: Vitamin C helps the body absorb non-haem iron from plant foods, improving how much iron is taken up.

cards.front: Which six minerals does this lesson cover?
cards.answer: Calcium / Iron / Sodium / Fluoride / Iodine / Phosphorus

cards.front: What five functions of water in the body does this lesson describe?
cards.answer: Waste elimination / Temperature regulation / Digestion / Nutrient transport / Chemical reactions

cards.front: Why does sweating help cool the body down?
cards.answer: When you are hot, the body produces sweat, and as it evaporates from the skin it cools you down.

cards.front: Why are fruit juice and smoothies capped at 150 ml a day, however much you drink?
cards.answer: Because of their high sugar content, drinking more than 150 ml does not count extra towards your fluid target.

title: The Eatwell Guide and Balanced Diets

cards.front: What are the five food groups on the Eatwell Guide?
cards.answer: Fruit and vegetables / Starchy carbohydrates (bread, rice, pasta, potatoes) / Dairy and alternatives / Beans, pulses, fish, eggs and meat / Oils and spreads
items: Beans, pulses, fish, eggs and meat

cards.front: Which four life stages does this lesson give nutrition advice for?
cards.answer: Children (2-11 years) / Teenagers (12-18 years) / Adults (19-64 years) / Elderly (65+ years)

cards.front: Why are smaller, nutrient-dense meals recommended for elderly people?
cards.answer: Their energy needs fall as they become less active, but their nutrient needs stay high.

cards.front: Why do dried fruit and fruit juice count as only one portion a day at most?
cards.answer: Drying and juicing concentrates the sugar and removes fibre, so more does not count as extra.

cards.front: What four main factors affect BMR, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Age / Gender / Body size / Muscle mass

cards.front: What three methods of nutritional analysis does this lesson describe?
cards.answer: Food composition tables / Nutritional analysis software / Food labels

cards.front: Why is nutritional analysis software useful for planning or modifying a dish?
cards.answer: It gives an instant nutrient breakdown and can flag where a dish is too high in fat, sugar or salt.

cards.front: Why can the body use protein for energy when carbohydrate and fat stores run low?
cards.answer: Protein is normally used for growth and repair, but becomes a back-up energy source once carbohydrate and fat run low.

cards.front: This lesson covers six diet-related health risks. What are they?
cards.answer: Obesity / Coronary heart disease / Bone diseases (rickets and osteoporosis) / Dental decay / Iron deficiency anaemia / Type 2 diabetes

cards.front: According to this lesson, obesity increases the risk of which four other conditions?
cards.answer: Type 2 diabetes / Coronary heart disease / Certain cancers / Joint problems

cards.front: Why are vegetarians and vegans at greater risk of iron deficiency anaemia?
cards.answer: The most easily absorbed iron (haem iron) comes from animal sources, so they rely on iron that is harder to absorb.

cards.front: Why does carrying excess body fat increase the risk of type 2 diabetes?
cards.answer: Excess body fat, especially around the abdomen, increases insulin resistance, so blood sugar stays high.

cards.front: What are the six conditions bacteria need to grow, remembered by the mnemonic FATTOM?
cards.answer: Food / Acidity / Time / Temperature / Oxygen / Moisture

cards.front: What are the four types of food contamination named in this lesson?
cards.answer: Microbiological contamination / Chemical contamination / Physical contamination / Allergenic contamination

cards.front: Why are pregnant women more at risk of infections such as Listeria?
cards.answer: Their immune systems are naturally suppressed to protect the baby, making them more susceptible to infection.

cards.front: Why is Clostridium perfringens linked to meat that is cooked, cooled slowly and then reheated?
cards.answer: It forms heat-resistant spores that survive cooking and can multiply if the food is cooled too slowly.

cards.front: What four main areas does food hygiene cover, according to this lesson?
cards.answer: Personal hygiene / Kitchen hygiene / Food storage / Cooking and temperature control

cards.front: What three types of date marking does this lesson describe?
cards.answer: Use-by date / Best-before date / Display-until date

cards.front: Why is an antibacterial product needed on work surfaces, not just washing-up liquid?
cards.answer: Washing-up liquid removes visible dirt but does not kill bacteria, so an antibacterial product is needed too.

cards.front: Why is it risky to reheat food more than once?
cards.answer: Each time food is cooled and reheated, it passes back through the danger zone, letting bacteria multiply again.

cards.front: What are the three medical conditions covered in this lesson's section on medical dietary needs?
cards.answer: Coeliac disease / Lactose intolerance / Nut allergy

cards.front: Which four nutrients does the traffic light labelling system show levels for?
cards.answer: Fat / Saturated fat / Sugar / Salt

cards.front: Why may low-income households have less varied diets?
cards.answer: Processed and convenience foods are often cheaper per calorie than fresh fruit and vegetables.

cards.front: Why are there restrictions on advertising high fat, salt and sugar foods to children?
cards.answer: Marketing has a powerful influence on young people, shaping what they choose to buy.

title: Food Science — Heat Transfer and Functional Properties

cards.front: This lesson describes four functional properties of protein in cooking. What are they?
cards.answer: Denaturation / Coagulation / Gluten formation / Foam formation

cards.front: What are the four types of raising agent described in this lesson?
cards.answer: Chemical / Mechanical / Steam / Biological

cards.front: Why does food cooked by radiation, such as grilling, need to be turned?
cards.answer: Radiation only heats the surface, so the food is turned, or the inside cooks by conduction from outside in.

cards.front: Why does steaming keep more of a vegetable's water-soluble vitamins than boiling?
cards.answer: In steaming, the food never touches the water, so fewer water-soluble vitamins are lost into it.

title: Food Provenance — Sustainability, Processing and Production

cards.front: What are the four main types of food additive described in this lesson?
cards.answer: Colourings / Flavourings / Preservatives / Emulsifiers and stabilisers

cards.front: Which four nutrients must white flour be fortified with by law?
cards.answer: Thiamin (vitamin B1) / Niacin (vitamin B3) / Calcium / Iron

cards.front: Why might a product grown in a heated UK greenhouse have a higher carbon footprint than an imported one grown outdoors?
cards.answer: Heating a greenhouse can use more energy than growing the same food outdoors abroad and shipping it by sea.

cards.front: Why are some artificial food colourings a cause for concern?
cards.answer: Some artificial colourings have been linked to hyperactivity in children.

cards.front: When comparing cuisines, this lesson says to look at which five areas?
cards.answer: Distinctive ingredients / Cooking methods / Equipment / Eating patterns / Presentation

cards.front: This lesson groups sensory tests into three categories. What are they?
cards.answer: Preference tests / Discrimination tests / Grading tests

cards.front: Why is coloured lighting avoided when running a sensory taste test?
cards.answer: It can disguise differences between the samples being tested.

cards.front: Why are individual booths used when carrying out sensory testing?
cards.answer: They stop tasters from influencing each other's judgements.
